WASHINGTON — At first glance, President Trump’s decision to relax U.S. sanctions on Russia despite its continuing invasion of Ukraine was a dramatic break from principles that guided American foreign policy for most of a century.
Since the end of World War II, U.S.-Russian relations have oscillated between hostility and friendship, but one element was consistent: When Russia tried to take over one of its neighbors, the United States pushed back.
This time, though, the United States appeared to favor the aggressor, not the victim .
“The Trump administration has abandoned any pretense of being an honest broker,” Richard N. Haass, a former senior State Department official under then-President George W. Bush, wrote last week. “It has gone all in on Russia’s side.”
The break from long-standing tradition was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
Trump has long expressed admiration for Russia’s autocratic leader, Vladimir Putin — part of a syndrome one of his former aides, Fiona Hill, has called “autocrat envy.”
“He wants to rule like them,” she said, referring to the president’s bromances with Putin, China’s Xi Jinping and other strongmen.
Trump’s push to end the war that has raged since 2022 comes as midterm elections could give Democrats control of Congress, expanding their oversight powers.
Meanwhile, Trump often expresses disdain for democratically elected leaders of smaller countries, and he reserves a special loathing for the president of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelensky.
He has repeatedly said Zelensky was foolish to resist Russia’s 2022 invasion because, in his view, the larger country is almost certain to win the war.
“Russia is a massive country,” he said this month. “Even if it loses a million soldiers, it still has a million more. Ukraine doesn’t have that kind of manpower.”
Moreover, Trump has long believed U.S. companies could reap an economic bonanza from Russia’s resource-rich economy. As a real estate magnate, he spent 30 years seeking deals in Moscow; in 2008, his son Donald Jr. said Russians had provided the Trump Organization “a lot of our assets.”
In the short run, the president hopes to boost Republican prospects in next week’s midterm elections by buying diesel fuel from Russia — a move aimed at lowering prices at the cost of bolstering Putin’s war economy. (It hasn’t worked; the price of diesel has risen slightly since Trump’s decision.)
But he has a longer-term goal as well. He has long believed better relations between the United States and Russia would be good for both countries, no matter who’s in power in Moscow. And he has long yearned openly for a Nobel Peace Prize — and one way might be to arrange a durable ceasefire in Ukraine.
All those factors have led Trump to overturn two major elements of traditional U.S. foreign policy.
Instead of supporting Ukraine, the victim of a foreign military invasion, he’s been pressing the Zelensky to accept Putin’s demands for territory.
“President Trump still wants a personal relationship with Putin, and he wants to change the nature of the bilateral U.S.-Russian relationship. Ukraine is in the way. So what President Trump is trying to do is get Ukraine out of the way. ... President Trump wants Zelensky to capitulate,” Hill said.
“Zelensky has to want to settle this war, and if he doesn’t, I think it’s going to be a very bad thing,” Trump said last week.
As he issued that advice, Ukraine’s army was experiencing interruptions with three forms of U.S. military help: Starlink, the communications system it uses to guide its anti-drone missiles; U.S.-provided early radar warnings of Russian missile attacks; and supplies of Patriot anti-missile weapons. U.S. officials claimed the three incidents were not deliberate — but to Ukrainians, they felt like a warning.
Meanwhile, instead of putting pressure on Putin through the traditional means of economic sanctions, Trump said he was trying to entice the Russian leader to negotiate by giving him preemptive rewards.
“I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don’t want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table,” he explained on Truth Social. “Great progress is being made.”
But signs of that progress were hard to find. In St. Petersburg last week, Trump’s personal envoy, Steve Witkoff, presented Putin with a ceasefire proposal that the Americans negotiated with Ukraine and European countries. A top Putin aide dismissed the document, saying it “contained little of real value.”
Instead, the Russian president offered to increase Russian fertilizer exports to U.S. farmers. And he said he hoped Trump would join him at a summit meeting in China with Xi.
President Vladimir Putin has agreed to resume trilateral negotiations with Washington and Kyiv to end the war in Ukraine, according to a Kremlin official.
Ukraine has not been invited to that meeting, which prompted Haass to resurrect an old diplomatic aphorism: “If you’re not at the table, you’re on the menu.”
Haass and other veterans of U.S. negotiations with Russia fear that Putin is merely stalling for time and pocketing Trump’s concessions while he tries to grind Ukraine down with missile attacks on Kyiv and other cities.
“If Trump and Witkoff were serious, they would give Putin 15 days to say yes to their ceasefire proposal — and if he doesn’t, they would impose new and tougher sanctions,” said Steven Pifer, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine. “There are still a lot of things they can do that would put Russia in a corner.”
But that has not been Trump’s inclination so far.
The irony, Hill said, is that even if Trump gets his way, that may not produce the victory he appears to expect.
“Putin and Trump are not the only actors in this,” she said. “Ukraine is not anybody’s to give. Its not Putin’s to have, and it’s not Zelensky’s. ... This whole war is about Ukrainians wanting the right to determine their own future. It’s not Putin’s right or anyone else’s. It’s not Donald Trump’s to give away.”

Nasdaq futures rebounded early Friday as some investors bought the dip in chip stocks following a punishing sell-off that sent the Nasdaq into correction territory.
A looming October jobs report kept a cap on the gains.
Nasdaq-100 futures bounced by 1.7%, S&P 500 futures rose 0.4%,  while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures remained under pressure, down by 0.9%.
Worries of a potential slowdown in data center construction following big Democratic wins in the House and Senate and key state governorships hit U.S. markets hard on Thursday.
The heavy selling Thursday sent the three major stock averages to their worst one-day losses since April 2025. The Nasdaq Composite tumbled 5.5%, closing more than 10% below its most recent high and putting it in what Wall Street regards as a correction. The broad-market S&P 500 lost 4.4%, while the Dow fell more than 1,800 points, or 3.4%.
All 11 sectors in the S&P 500 closed lower, but shares of companies tied to the AI build-out led the decline.
In early trading Friday, shares of Micron were up 9% following a 17% decline on Thursday. Nvidia was up 5% after a 9% rout the day before.
"The scale of the falls in some of the market's biggest names has been striking. But it also highlights the concentration risk that has built up in U.S. equity markets," Stuart Clark, portfolio manager at Quilter, said by email.
"With a relatively small number of technology and semiconductor stocks now carrying so much weight, weakness in those names quickly translates into sizeable falls for the Nasdaq and S&P 500."
The Magnificent Seven stocks shed a $1 trillion in total market capitalization on Thursday alone. Along with Nvidia, Amazon, Tesla and Alphabet were in the green on Friday.
Another market catalyst awaits investors Friday morning when the Bureau of Labor Statistics releases the October nonfarm payrolls report. The Dow Jones consensus estimate among economists anticipates that employers added 59,000 jobs last month, while the national unemployment rate held steady at 4.2%.
All three major averages are poised for losses on the week, even after Wednesday's big rally in the wake of the election. The Nasdaq is off by some 4.4% and the S&P 500 by almost 3% through Thursday. The 30-stock Dow is the outperformer, lower by just 0.5% week to date.
Oil prices rebounded a touch on Friday, extending earlier gains, as investors weighed the risk of renewed military escalation between the U.S. and Iran following the midterm elections, alongside prospects for a diplomatic breakthrough.
International benchmark Brent crude futures were recently higher by 36 cents, or 0.39%, to $98.65 a barrel,  having jumped to almost $100 a barrel earlier in the session. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures were ahead 43 cents or 0.48% to $90.98 a barrel.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 index was 1.26% lower in early deals, following deep losses in Asia-Pacific markets on Friday and a sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday .
All sectors were in the red, though technology saw among the smallest impact, down 0.8%. Media stocks tumbled 2.4% as health-care fell 2.2%.
The sharp sell-off in AI-related names this week reflects an adjustment in growth expectations to a more sustainable level, according to William de Gale, co-founder and lead portfolio manager at Blue Box Asset Management — but it does not change "insatiable" levels of demand.
De Gale told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" that the technology sector had been delivering consistent profits and stock price growth of around 15% for nearly two decades. This was connected to a host of supply constraints, including in semiconductor equipment, raw materials, energy, staffing and permitting, which cap the growth rate, he said.
"AI has been able to grow a lot faster than that in recent years because it's been a lot smaller. It's a subset of the tech sector by and large, but eventually it becomes big enough that it runs into that overall constraint, and I think that's really what's happening now," de Gale said.
"The industry seems to be ahead of what expectations are, ahead of what is sustainable, and at the moment, all the models have 30% top line growth in them, going many years into the future, and nothing that big can grow that fast very long, so those models all need to come down to 15, to 20%, and that's the adjustment that's happening at the moment."
"I don't think there's any real issue with demand. The demand is insatiable, and the demand outside AI is pretty much insatiable as well."
Asia-Pacific markets tumbled on Friday, as a sharp sell-off in technology stocks swept across the region.
South Korea's Kospi fell more than 6%, leading losses in the region to end at 5,059.69, and declining 11.7% this week. The small-cap, tech-focused Kosdaq fell 5.03%, closing at 644.27.
Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 5.96% to 57,434.77, entering bear market territory.
Mainland China's CSI 300 fell 1.44% lower at 4,054.28, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng was down 1.32% as of its last hour of trade.
Taiwan's Taiex also entered bear market, dropping 4.51% to 39,701.64. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was down 0.49% at 9,020.8.
Germany's Daimler Truck reported an 89% year-on-year increase in earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) to 1.05 billion euros ($1.18 billion).
North American truck sales jumped 51%, which the company attributed to both a continued market recovery and the impact of tariff uncertainty in the same quarter last year. The North American market for heavy-duty trucks fell 7% in the first three quarters, but was offset by 8% growth in Europe.
Daimler, one of the world's biggest truck manufacturers, flagged ongoing market challenges, including slowing growth, rising energy costs and uncertainty in the global economy.
CFO Eva Scherer said the company showed "discipline in converting performance into cash" in the quarter and was "determined to maintain that discipline."
The U.S. is likely to resume military action against Iran in the coming days, a move that could send oil prices sharply higher, according to Bob McNally, CEO at geopolitical and energy analysis firm Rapidan Energy Group.
Speaking to CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ," McNally put the odds of "a resumption of military fighting" at 80% as the U.S. midterm elections recede.
McNally said he expects both Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude futures to rise above $100 a barrel. The benchmarks are currently trading at about $100 and $91, respectively.
"President Donald Trump is determined, as a legacy item, almost at all costs, to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, having them give up their nuclear capabilities," McNally said.
"The Iranian regime, on the other hand, is not willing to do it. And as long as that core difference in that deal space is absent, the escalation dynamic remains in place," he added.

South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix plunged over 8%, while Samsung Electronics shed 7%. LG Innotek and LG Display fell 10% and 7.7%, respectively, as selling pressure spread across the country's technology sector.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo’s Latin America trip will take him above 11,000 feet, weeks after lung cancer surgery
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo’s Latin America trip will take him above 11,000 feet, weeks after lung cancer surgery
articles.content_orig:
Just over three weeks ago, the most significant visit of Pope Leo’s pontificate looked to be in doubt. The 71-year-old’s lung cancer surgery led some in the Vatican to believe his trip to Latin America would be postponed or its intense schedule adjusted.
But Leo XIV is forging ahead with a grueling 12-day visit, which includes Uruguay, Argentina, and an emotional “homecoming” to Peru, the country where he served as a missionary and bishop for around two decades.
He plans to cover a lot of ground – around 19,000 miles – while in Latin America. From November 6 to 17, the pope is scheduled to take 14 flights (including two in a helicopter), give 36 speeches and participate in around 50 events in what is one of the most intense papal trips of recent years.
He will also visit Cusco, Peru, which is more than 11,000 feet above sea-level and where there is 35% less oxygen per breath. During the whole trip, he’ll travel to 10 cities, preside at large open-air Masses and vigils and meet with political leaders.
The trip, especially Cusco’s altitude, has raised questions about his health and the precautions being taken while there. It has also shone a light on a region that has profoundly shaped him and set his path to the papacy.
The pontiff had surgery last month to remove a third of his right lung after a small growth was discovered during routine checks, which was later confirmed as cancer. His surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, said afterward that there were “no clinical reasons why this visit should not take place,” and doctors have said he does not need further treatment.
Vatican officials told reporters that Pope Leo will have a medical team available to him for the trip but stressed that no special measures are being taken. “We’re speaking of a 71-year-old person in good health,” the Vatican spokesman said ahead of the visit.
He explained the pope will travel with the “ordinary medical assistance,” including doctors, nurses and an ambulance, which usually travels with the pope’s convoy. But the spokesman said he wasn’t going into too much detail as the pope does not have a “permanent condition.” And if the Vatican medical team needs any help, one of the journalists traveling with the pope is also a doctor.
Montse Alvarado, the new head of Vatican Communications, told journalists on Tuesday that the pope’s “stamina is fantastic,” and that “he’ll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen.”
Dr. Matthew Triplette, a pulmonologist from the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center in Seattle, told CNN the risk of a medical emergency during the trip is “low” but that this could include “either a collapsed lung or blood clots.”
Triplette said the pope may be advised to “take low-dose blood thinners or use exercises or compression devices” to lower the possibility of blood clots in his legs when flying, which could cause major issues if they spread to the lungs. He added that the pope may feel more fatigue with exertion, particularly because there is less oxygen available at altitude.
In the aftermath of his surgery, many speculated that the trip would be canceled.
“I must confess that, until just a few days ago, I was among the few who had serious doubts about whether this trip could even take place,” Guzmán Carriquiry, a Uruguayan former Vatican official who worked on Latin American issues for nearly 50 years in the church’s central administration, told reporters on Tuesday.
But he also pointed out that the pope’s health team gave him the green light. “This suggests that his doctors believe the pope possesses a robust physical constitution; it also serves as a testament to the pope’s ardent desire and determination to go out and meet our people,” he said.
But Carriquiry noted that he would have removed Cusco from the agenda if he had organized the trip.
While Leo XIV is known for his gentle, low-key style, he is determined.
Answering a question from CNN, Alvarado said the pope “personally confirmed this trip with no changes,” and that he was looking forward to returning to Latin America.
The continent, and Peru in particular, is close to his heart, and Alvarado said the pope would speak off the cuff frequently in Spanish, a language he is fluent in.
“He’s going on this trip very simply because he wants to go,” is how Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican foreign minister, put it at an event in Rome at the end of last month.
The Peruvian part of the trip will be emotional, as Leo arrives there “as an adopted brother, adopted by the Peruvian people,” said Carriquiry.
The pope, who remains a Peruvian citizen, had three stints in Peru, having first arrived there in his 30s. He also served as Bishop of Chiclayo in the northwest part of the country from 2015 to 2023.
The pope will return to Chiclayo during the trip and is expected to receive a rapturous welcome. Leo is remembered fondly in the city, where he was considered a hands-on bishop who was known to travel across his diocese on horseback.
“The pope spent many years living amongst the simple, poor and devout people of rural Latin America in northern Peru, as a missionary and a pastor,” Carriquiry, who is the former secretary of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, said.
Leo is expected to draw huge crowds when he’s there, with estimates of around 1.2 million people expected to attend his final Mass of the trip at Las Palmas Airbase in Lima.
He is also expected to draw huge crowds in Argentina, where more than a million people are expected to attend his Mass in Buenos Aires.
The late Pope Francis, the first Argentine pontiff, never made a visit to his home country, so Leo’s visit is one that is generating intense interest.
Francis never gave a clear reason as to why he didn’t visit Argentina. Carriquiry, a close friend of the late pope, said it “remains an enigma.”
Leo XIV’s visit will underline his plans to continue the reforms of his predecessor, but with his own distinctive style.
The pope’s visit comes at a time when Argentine President Javier Milei’s “chainsaw” austerity measures have led to welfare spending cuts. Milei has also equated state-led social justice programs with communism.
Pope Leo, in contrast, has made the church’s social teaching and concern for the marginalized a central concern of his papacy. His itinerary includes a visit to a federal prison in Buenos Aires and a stop at a care center for people with intellectual and physical disabilities in Claypole which has been affected by the Milei cuts.
Both Milei and Peru’s President Keiko Fujimori are notable figures in Latin America’s right-wing surge. They also enjoy support from the Trump administration, which Leo has publicly disagreed with — particularly on migration issues.
Leo XIV would not have been elected pope had he not been sent to Peru as a young Augustinian missionary.
His time in Latin America put him on a path to be spotted by Pope Francis. It was Francis who appointed the then-Rev. Robert Prevost as bishop in Chiclayo before later bringing him to Rome and naming him a cardinal.
All of this set him up as a candidate in the 2025 conclave. While Leo is the first pope from the United States and grew up in Chicago, his experience in Latin America has profoundly influenced his outlook.
In Peru, he served in the birthplace of liberation theology, a movement focused on social and political action to help the poor and oppressed. As a bishop, he was known for organizing practical assistance for those affected by floods or in need of medical equipment during the Covid-19 pandemic.
He served in a church in Peru which emphasized an inclusive model, giving greater roles to those not ordained as priests and bishops, including women.
Leo’s time in Peru also saw him exposed to the fallout of the clerical abuse crisis, including a major scandal involving a powerful Catholic group . The Vatican says the pope will have two meetings with abuse survivors during his trip, one in Argentina and another in Peru.

articles.title_orig: Mystery Seller Seeks to Dump $500 Million of Data Center Loans
articles.title_zh: Mystery Seller Seeks to Dump $500 Million of Data Center Loans
articles.content_orig:
ING is reportedly seeking buyers for a portfolio of 12 data center loans worth around $500 million, joining a broader push by banks to distribute credit risk tied to the artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out.
The auction is said to include a $25 million piece linked to the Stargate project in New Mexico, which involves OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle , as well as certain other loan assets involving Vantage Data Centers and CyrusOne, Bloomberg reported Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.
ING will hold a bids-wanted-in-competition, or BWIC, auction process, with bids sized at $10 million or more due by Nov. 19, according to Bloomberg. A BWIC is a competitive process for investors to bid on pieces of a loan portfolio.
An ING spokesperson declined to comment.
The sale highlights a growing market for banks to move data center loans to private credit firms, asset managers and insurers as financing for the AI boom expands.
Investment banks typically use a lend-to-distribute model for these types of loans, said Hank Calenti, global markets strategist at SMBC.
"The buyers can range from private credit investors through asset managers to insurers. They would buy these assets for their expected higher returns," he said.
The ING sale comes as fears grow over soaring debt tied to the AI build-out — and potentially disappointing returns among investors.
Those concerns have accelerated following the Democrats' sweeping win in the U.S. midterms, which could see moratoriums or tighter restrictions on data center construction in certain states.
The perceived risk of a construction slowdown sent AI-related stocks into free fall on Thursday, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closing the session down 5.5% — its worst day since April 2025 — and into correction territory .
"Whether banks sell more based on AI data centers moratorium fears should be driven by the cost (discount received) versus the benefit of exiting to free up cash for further lending, where the cost includes explaining the exposure to your board," Calenti told CNBC via email.
"This could be business as usual, or financiers looking to exit before the door shuts."
Pruksa Iamthongthong, head of APAC equities at Aberdeen Investments, said the Democrats' gains have increased concerns around greater scrutiny of data center development, at a time when investors were already questioning the financing and returns behind the scale of AI capital spending.
"We think near-term volatility could continue as the market assesses potential delays to U.S. data center construction and constraints around compute capacity."
Earlier this year, Wall Street lenders including JPMorgan Chase and Morgan Stanley were said to be exploring a variety of approaches to reduce their lending exposures to data center construction.
According to a Financial Times report on May 3, these include offloading portions of debt via private sales to non-bank lenders, as well as through so-called significant risk transfers, which transfer part of a bank's credit risk to investors to free up balance sheet capacity.

articles.content_orig:
• Bomb threats forced the diversion of more than a dozen flights across Europe on Thursday, the latest in a string of incidents disrupting airspace. Several authorities have said no devices have been found.
• Four of the flight diversions were in the Czech Republic. The bomb threats were made in an anonymous email and other airports received the email too, a representative of the Václav Havel Airport in Prague told CNN .
• A company linked to Rome’s airport received an email from a group purporting to be anti-feminist and calling itself the Male State that claimed there were bombs on two flights. But it is unconfirmed who was behind the wave of threats and the EU says it is too early to say they are linked.
Our live coverage of this story has ended. Read more here.
Passengers at Rome Fiumicino airport said they would go ahead with their travels on Thursday, after bomb threats that turned out to be false impacted two flights bound for the Italian capital.
One affected flight from Dublin was diverted to Normandy in France, whilst the other, from Helsinki, was escorted safely into Rome airport by Italian air force fighter jets.
The airport operator ADR conducted searches and said there was no threat, according to Reuters.
Watch the video to hear how passengers are reacting.
While it remains unclear who is responsible for the spate of bomb threats across Europe this week, one aviation expert said he is looking closely at Russia.
“From a geopolitical view, I’m thinking, you always have to think about the scenario of hybrid warfare, where a country in this way — today we are looking at Russia, right? — is attacking us on multiple fronts, from railways to supermarkets to blood banks, most recently,” Eric Schouten, head of the aviation security ⁠group Dyami, told Reuters.
“The energy sector, the internet sector, and the aviation sector are among those,” he added.
Russia has recently been accused by Denmark, Poland and Romania of causing disruption through hybrid attacks - hostile action that targets and destabilizes an adversary through a blend of non-military tactics and cyber assaults on essential infrastructure.
The unconventional mixture of techniques used in such an attack makes it difficult to trace back to a single actor, he said.
Denmark, Poland and Romania are also among the nations impacted by Thursday’s disruptions, and Schouten pointed out that those affected have supported Ukraine during Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Earlier Thursday, CNN affiliate SKYTG24 published an email from an anti-feminist group calling itself “The Male State” which appeared to reveal the origin of a false bomb threat claims made regarding two flights bound for an airport in Rome.
The International Centre for Counter-Terrorism, a Netherlands-based think tank, said “The Male State” was created in Russia in 2016.
“It transitioned from being one of the most notorious misogynist movements in Russia to one of the main online supporters and promoters of the war in Ukraine,” the report said .
Russia has denied engaging in hybrid warfare.
Passengers and crew on at least 14 planes have been impacted by bomb threats in Europe today, with multiple flights rerouted and some having to be escorted by fighter jets.
All the threats have so far proven false, and there’s no clear indication who’s behind them, but they are causing considerable disruption.
Here’s a running CNN tally of flights affected, based on information from airlines and regional officials:
Matthew Bojarsky’s LOT Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Paris was taxiing to the runway when the pilot announced it had been cancelled for safety reasons.
Passengers were told the plane would wait at the end of the runway for “some officers,” he told CNN, after posting a video on X that shows men in military fatigues outside the plane.
Eventually the flight, one of more than a dozen to face bomb threats on Thursday,  was continued on a different plane.
“We were moved into a hall, then waited for four hours,” Bojarsky said. “We got the information from the news, the pilot said it was ‘safety protocol’.”
Officials at the Madrid-Barajas Airport in Spain’s capital received a “bomb threat” naming three flights on Thursday, airport operator AENA said.
Law enforcement teams carried out an assessment “and the relevant security checks” and found nothing on board, a spokesperson for AENA told CNN.
An anti-feminist group calling itself “The Male State” emailed bomb threats to a logistics company working with Rome Fiumicino Airport on Thursday naming two flights bound for the Italian capital.
The email, first published by CNN Affiliate SkyTG24, made the false claim that “explosive devices” had been placed on two flights – one from Helsinki and another from Dublin. A spokesperson for the airport confirmed to CNN the screenshot was authentic.
“You’re all complicit in a criminal plot, we want to annihilate you for this,” the memo read in Italian. “We, the fighters of the Male State, with our actions will leave a mark on history. Your feminist regime will never forget it.”
Earlier on Thursday , Italian air force fighter jets escorted the Finnair flight from Helsinki safely into Rome airport. A second flight from Dublin to Rome, operated by the Irish airline, Aer Lingus, was diverted to Normandy, northern France.
The email went to Aviapartner, a Belgium-based logistics company providing luggage services to the Rome airport.
The email alias appeared to be linked to the municipality of the Colombian capital Bogotá, whose mayor Luis Fernando Galan told CNN his team was working to establish what happened.
“It could be the account was hacked, we’ve had several of them before,” Galan told CNN.
Aviapartner declined to comment to CNN.
The EU transport commissioner said it is “too early” to determine whether the bomb threats that caused several flights to be diverted and others escorted to their scheduled destination across Europe this week are connected.
“It is too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked,” Apostolos Tzitzikostas said in a statement released Thursday, “National investigations remain ongoing.”
The commissioner said that the situation is being closely monitored, and that the department is “in contact with the affected member states and the European Aviation Safety Agency.”
“The EU-level information sharing mechanism has been activated related to aviation security,” it added.
The commissioner said any threat against civilians is “unacceptable,” and said all relevant bodies have been liaising to ensure aviation safety and security is not compromised.
While no explosive devices have yet been found following bomb threats, the motivation behind the reports remains unclear.
The UK’s transport minister says the bomb threats that have caused several flights to be diverted and others escorted to their destinations are a “malicious hoax.”
Speaking to British media, Heidi Alexander said that the disrupted flights had triggered “established processes for dealing with hoax and malicious threats, and that’s what these threats have been.”
While the minister insisted that the British government is taking the threats seriously, she added “we understand these have been malicious hoax threats.”
At least 14 flights have been impacted by the threats Thursday. No explosives have yet been found.
Bulgaria’s transport authorities are the latest to confirm that their inspections found no issues on any of the three aircraft that were the subject of this morning’s bomb threats.
Two Ryanair flights to Sofia from Madrid and Copenhagen respectively landed safely at their destination after the bomb threats.
Another Ryanair flight from London was diverted to Plovdiv, southeast of the capital, following a threat.
“Upon landing, the necessary inspections were carried out in accordance with the applicable procedures and no issues were identified,” a spokesperson for Bulgaria’s transport ministry told CNN Thursday.

Taxpayers age 65 and older, as well as those who are blind, can claim an additional standard deduction . For 2027, that additional amount is $1,700 ($2,100 if unmarried and not a surviving spouse).
Those eligible can add the extra standard deduction to the regular amount for their filing status. A single taxpayer 65 or older (or who is blind) can claim a total standard deduction of $18,700 on their 2027 federal tax return.

Your standard deduction amount might differ if you can be claimed as a dependent on another taxpayer’s federal tax return.

articles.title_orig: China's Macau jails ex-lawmaker in first national security trial
articles.title_zh: China's Macau jails ex-lawmaker in first national security trial
articles.content_orig:
Au was sentenced to 12 years and six months' jail for "subversion against the political power of the state"
Macau has sentenced an ex-lawmaker and pro-democracy campaigner to 12 years and six months' jail in the city's first national security case.
Following a closed-door trial, Au Kam San, 69, was convicted on Friday of "subversion against the political power of the state", among other offences.
His wife Virginia Cheang condemned the ruling, calling the case a "groundless persecution designed to humiliate Au".
Macau was handed back to China in 1999, ending over 400 years of Portuguese administration. Its national security law came into effect in 2009, criminalising acts of treason, secession, and subversion against the Chinese Communist Party.
The law was revised in 2023, broadening its scope to include non-violent acts of secession, and again this year, to allow for trials to be held behind closed doors.
Prosecutors had accused Au of assisting and collaborating with "external hostile organisations" by collecting, preparing and disseminating information that was "manifestly filled with political claims of a subversive nature against the state".
These took place "over a long period of time", the prosecutors claim.
Au was arrested in July 2025 and later charged with three counts of subverting the state's power, three counts of endangering national security by establishing contact with foreign organisations, and one count of breach of confidentiality.
He was found guilty of four of the seven charges following a three-day trial which ended in September. A judge had ordered that the trial be held behind closed doors "to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the interests of national security".
Macau's authorities never publicly disclosed the details of the case. Au's family had earlier told the media Au was not allowed to seek his own legal representation and had instead been assigned a lawyer by the court.
Au's wife Cheang said she hoped authorities would grant her and her family permission to regularly write to and visit Au in prison.
"I dare not hope for more as I believe that will only lead to greater disappointment," she said in an open letter on Friday.
Au, who was formerly a primary school teacher, was elected to the Legislative Assembly in September 2001. For 20 years, he served as one of only a handful of pro-democracy lawmakers in the legislature, largely made up of pro-Beijing loyalists.
Au had co-organised annual vigils in Macau to commemorate the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
These vigils were previously tolerated in places like Macau and Hong Kong, but have effectively been banned in both cities since China imposed a sweeping national security law on Hong Kong in 2020.
Au's jailing comes a day after Hong Kong sentenced Joshua Wong, the face of its now-quashed democracy movement, to 10 years in jail . Wong, 30, whose activism started when he was just a teen, has been in custody for the last six years.

articles.title_orig: Why is Iran exempting India, China, Qatar, Iraq from Hormuz restrictions?
articles.title_zh: Why is Iran exempting India, China, Qatar, Iraq from Hormuz restrictions?
articles.content_orig:
Iran has exempted ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar from its Strait of Hormuz restrictions, a senior Iranian lawmaker said on Tuesday.
“Ships from these countries pass freely, and the Americans do not intercept them either,” Amir Hayat Moqaddam, deputy chairman of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told the Iranian Students’ News Agency (ISNA).
Iran effectively shut the strait early in the US-Israel war on Iran , which began on February 28, and the United States reimposed a naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports in July.
So why have these four countries been granted passage through the critical strait, and can their ships really sail freely while the blockade remains in place?
It will receive medicine from India and political backing from China, according to Hayat Moqaddam. Iran already receives diplomatic support from Qatar, which is leading mediation efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran.
Hayat Moqaddam said Tehran will also collect transit fees from Indian and Chinese ships, while Qatari vessels pass free. He did not say whether Iraqi ships will pay a toll.
“Whatever the lawmaker says is the rationale – the big question is if it works and, if yes, to what extent?” Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst and affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies, told Al Jazeera.
“Iran has been under sanctions for a very long time, so bartering and quid pro quos in trade are nothing new,” he said. The difference now, he added, is that “it’s about poking holes in an embargo and getting crucial goods/services in and out”.
Nader Hashemi, an associate professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, said that “most likely Iran is charging a transit fee or a percentage of the cargo value to allow those ships to go through without being harassed”.
“It’s a clever move by Tehran for several reasons,” Wolfgang Pusztai, a security and defence analyst and Austria’s former defence attache to Libya, told Al Jazeera.
“If successful, this move will generate significant revenue for Iran, as China is by far the largest purchaser of Iranian crude oil, buying nearly 90 percent of Iran’s total oil exports,” he said.
By including Qatar, with its many liquefied natural gas (LNG) buyers, and India, Iran is also “trying to undermine acceptance” of Washington’s strategy in the conflict, especially as it charges Qatar no tolls, he added.
All four are highly dependent on the Strait of Hormuz for exports.
Of the 10.23 million barrels a day of Gulf crude that passed through the strait in October, about 42 percent went to China and 13 percent to India, Muyu Xu, a senior crude oil analyst at the analytics firm Kpler, told Al Jazeera.
“China is the country most able to cross US interests. The question is whether Beijing considers it worth the potential political cost,” Parsi said.
Asia is particularly reliant on Gulf oil and gas usually shipped out via Hormuz. Countries there have much to offer in return for allowing ships to pass.
“For India, the shutdown of oil from the Gulf has been a great loss – and it is a big producer of the pharmaceuticals that Iran cannot manufacture itself,” he said.
Qatar, which is mediating between Washington and Tehran, shipped no LNG through the strait in August, but managed 1.8 million tonnes in October, Xu said.
Its crude transits fell over the same period, from 517,000 barrels a day to 193,000, while Iraq’s rose from 1.69 million to 2.65 million.
Kpler has been unable to trace the origin of up to two million barrels a day of Middle Eastern crude, so both countries’ flows may be higher, Xu said.
“India and Qatar have closer relationships with DC they need to maintain – while both of them also feel let down by Trump,” Parsi said, adding, “For Qatar, maintaining a relationship with Iran is also vital since it’s an unavoidable neighbour.”
“So for all of them, there are upsides for these exemptions from Iranian restrictions but also political dangers,” he said.
Iran began letting some vessels from countries it considers friendly pass within weeks of the war starting. And in April, its military command said “brotherly” Iraq was exempt.
With the Iraqi exemption, Iran “probably intends to support the economic recovery” of its western neighbour, a fellow Shia-majority country, Pusztai said.
That depends on Washington.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) has said the blockade applies to “all vessels of all nations entering or leaving coastal areas or ports in Iran”, while vessels avoiding Iranian ports are not affected.
It has also said humanitarian shipments, including “food and medical supplies essential for the survival of the civilian populations”, can pass after inspection.
But Hayat Moqaddam did not appear to limit the exemptions to ships trading with other Gulf states, Pusztai noted. “If this is really the case, this would also have a significant impact on the other Gulf states, including Saudi Arabia,” he said.
“This could make the continuation of the American naval blockade more difficult and less effective, assuming Washington accepts this Iranian move,” he said. The main change, he added, is that the exemption “would also cover Chinese/Indian ships from/to Iran”, if the US accepts it.
It is also unclear whether “ships of these countries” means the flag a vessel flies, its owner, its operator or some other link, Pusztai said.
Ending the blockade is one of Tehran’s demands before it will commit to broader peace talks with the US, which will include discussions about Iran’s nuclear programme. Qatar-mediated talks currently centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait if the US meets seven conditions, including this and lifting sanctions.
“It seems to be that Iran tries to separate the questions of free passage through the Strait of Hormuz and oil exports from the nuclear question,” Pusztai said, adding, “The American reaction will show if this is successful.”
“I think they make only limited difference at present,” Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG Group, told Al Jazeera.
“Markets are back to pricing in a peace deal, but if conflict flares up at full tilt, then Iranian commanders may not have time to distinguish their targets,” he said, adding: “At present, the focus remains squarely on the prospects of a broader deal.”
An exemption has not guaranteed safety. On October 30, the Qatari LNG carrier Al Mayeda was struck by “unidentified objects” in the Gulf, said its owner, Qatar Gas Transport Company.
More than 120 commercial ships have been hit in the region since the war began, with October being the worst month, according to data from the International Maritime Organization and United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations.

articles.title_orig: Officials search for the bear that killed a mother and daughter in British Columbia
articles.title_zh: Officials search for the bear that killed a mother and daughter in British Columbia
articles.content_orig:
Selah Reed's family first knew something was wrong when the 20-year-old missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister.
When no one had heard from Reed or her mother, Jenny Balcarras, by the next morning, they asked the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to check on their home in Bella Coola on British Columbia's central coast. Balcarras' car was gone and the doors were locked. They found the car at a trailhead up the road, but Balcarras and Reed were nowhere to be found.
Family members across Canada and the U.S. started mobilizing. Jenny Balcarras' brother, Matt, headed north from Vancouver Island, and his brother left from Calgary. They met and drove through the night but got a call late Monday that their sister had been killed, likely by a grizzly.
When they arrived at the trailhead Tuesday morning, ready to join the search for Reed, her remains had also been found . The search was now a tragic recovery effort.
The killings of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter happened only 3 to 4 kilometers (1.8 to 2.4 miles) from where a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and teachers last year as they walked on a trail. Eleven were injured, two of them critically, in the Nov. 20, 2025, attack.
Jeff Tyre, an inspector with the Conservation Officer Service, said that aggressive bear was never captured, but officials were able to collect its DNA. Officials have set new traps in the hopes of catching the bear involved in last weekend's attack and to learn whether it was the same bear from a year ago. They also are not sure whether more than one bear was involved.
Terry Webber, chief administrative officer for the Nuxalk Nation, said the killings were triggering for the families who were traumatized by last year's attack.
"Our community is still healing," he said, adding that they've imposed a curfew and are providing mental health services for the community. "Our priority is to ensure they're safe and ensure our community is supported."
The delay in finding the remains of the two women was complicated by difficult terrain, even though it was close to the trailhead, and the grizzly bear's behavior.
Searchers found Jenny Balcarras first, then her daughter. The search was helped by more resources and a cadaver dog, Matt Balcarras said.
Searchers found his niece's remains in a bear cache - a place where bears stash food, sometimes by digging a small hole and covering it with branches and vegetation to keep other animals and birds away.
"Even though it was within 100 or so meters (330 feet), locating remains in a cache is difficult," he said.
By the time officials located his niece, she could only be identified by her clothing, he said. His sister was in a similar condition, but they knew who she was thanks to several tiny tattoos, he said.
"There's no obvious body to identify," he said. "The coroner's investigation will include DNA and dental work. But there is no doubt that the remains that were found are theirs."
Grizzly bears are common in the area surrounding the Bella Coola community, officials said. Conservation officials maintain a hotline where people can report problem bears, but no calls had been received recently, Tyre said during a media briefing.
Balcarras, an art therapist, had moved to Bella Coola during the summer. She had previously lived in Alaska, where her children were born, and was "the central organizing person in our family," Matt Balcarras said.
"In classic, strong single-mother style, she scraped together a career and a life for herself and her kids," Balcarras said. She was small in stature but strong in character and physical abilities, he said.
She was comfortable living among the wildlife, he said.
"She lived in the Bush when her kids were babies," he said. "She and my niece were not naive or foolish or uninformed. They've lived in these areas and have been around animals of countless types for years and years and decades."
There are between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears estimated to live in British Columbia, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks . The species is classified as vulnerable. Conflicts between grizzly bears and humans are considered "relatively rare," the ministry said, unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs or food. Still, there have been a number of grizzly bear attacks in the province in recent years.
In October 2025, a grizzly bear injured two hikers in British Columbia's McGregor Mountain area, northeast of Prince George. One of the hikers was transported to the hospital in critical condition and died a few weeks later due to complications from the injuries. The grizzly bear was later found dead, according to the B.C. Conservation Officer Service.
A man suffered "significant injuries," including broken bones and lacerations, after being attacked by a grizzly bear while hunting in British Columbia's Elkford region in May 2024. He was able to shoot the bear to defend himself. The animal was later found dead. The man was flown to an area hospital for treatment.
A 21-year-old woman was seriously injured by a grizzly bear near Tumbler Ridge in British Columbia in July 2023. Authorities described the incident as a "defensive attack." The victim was transported via helicopter to an area hospital.
Ahmad  Mukhtar contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Japan’s Nikkei Breaks Below Key 60,000 Level on AI Selloff
articles.content_orig:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news, as Asia-Pacific markets slide after Wall Street rout
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.
Fears that the Democratic Party’s blue wave in this week’s midterm elections will sink the AI investment boom are roiling markets, following heavy losses on Wall Street last night.
Asia-Pacific markets are a sea of red (unlike the US election map on Tuesday night!), as investors ditch tech stocks after more than $3.2tn was wiped off the US stock market yesterday.
Today, Japan’s Nikkei stock index has slumped by almost 6% – its worst drop since April 7 2025 during the ‘liberation day’ tariff panic.
South Korea’s KOSPI is down 6.7%, and Taiwan’s TAIEX has dropped by 4.5% in a broad rout.
Christopher Forbes , head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets , called the market action “a bit of a disaster”, explaining ( via Reuters ):
double quotation mark “(Clients) were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out.
“All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints, ... because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome and you’re telling them, look, you’ve just lost money.
“And it’s not just a slap in terms of valuation. It’s basically a whole policy and six-year structural shift that says we’re now going to pause, we’re now going to cool AI, we’re now going to cool data centres, approvals and equity capital markets.”
After months of warnings that AI valuations were too high, and that the bubble might burst, US investors dashed to the exits en masse yesterday. The Nasdaq tech index slumped by 5.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) dropped 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, and the S&P 500 lost 4.36%.
Memory chip makers, who had been profiting from the AI boom, led the fallers – SanDisk slumped 22% and both Micron and AMD lost 17% of their value.
Chip giant Nvidia led the fallers on the DJIA , down over 9%.
Analysts pointed to policy uncertainty as Democrats are more critical of data centres, which could slow the rollout of AI investment – especially given public opposition to the sector .
Kyle Rodda , senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, says it was a “brutal sell-off” as fears about the future of the AI buildout gripped the markets.
double quotation mark The tumble in tech stocks that took hold in the immediate aftermath of the US midterm elections resumed as investors contemplated what a Democrat-controlled Congress may mean for tech regulation and the overall AI boom.
The regulatory and political risks arise at a time when the proverbial AI trade was already on shakier foundations. Earnings season has been an overall disappointment for the markets, with Magnificent Seven results so far undershooting growth expectations and flashing warning signs that the pace of AI spending is slowing down.
So, it could be a ‘tin hats on’ day in the markets. Investors will also be watching the latest US jobs report, for clues into the health of America’s labour market.
7am GMT: Lloyds house price index
9am GMT: UN’s FAO food price index
1.30pm GMT: US non-farm payrolls jobs report
3pm GMT: University of Michigan’s US consumer confidence report
Interestingly, Jefferies economist Mohit Kumar doesn’t believe yesterday’s losses are “the start of the unwind of the AI trade”.
double quotation mark We do admit that policy uncertainty after the Blue Tsunami raises concerns over AI investment and the pace of data center buildup.
However, data centers and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move onto other states or outside the country. AI investment has been a key driver of US growth, and we do not see Democrats as giving up on this growth engine.
There was a huge slump in the most AI-exposed parts of the US stock market yesterday, Jim Reid of Deutche Bank told clients this morning:
double quotation mark In fact, the scale of the moves ranked among the biggest in years, and the Philly semiconductor index (-12.25%) had its worst day since the pandemic slump in March 2020 . And in turn, that cascaded elsewhere, with the S&P 500 (-4.36%) posting its biggest slump since the Liberation Day volatility in April 2025 .
So that drove a huge surge in the VIX index (+11.6pts), which also saw its biggest daily jump since the Liberation Day period, ending the session at 28.2pts, its highest since March.
Mohit Kumar, economist at investent bank Jefferies , doesn’t expect a quick rebound from yesterday’s losses.
double quotation mark In previous episodes of retail selling, institutional investors have stepped in to find value. The approaching year-end complicates the behaviour of institutional accounts as risk appetite would be limited….
The geopolitical uncertainty around possible US action in Iran also suggests that investors would not rush to add risk.
Stuart Clark , portfolio manager at Quilter , points out that the dominance of the tech sector exacerbated yesterday’s selloff:
double quotation mark “The blue wave at the ballot box has quickly been replaced by a sea of red on investors’ screens. Technology stocks have sold off sharply, with the immediate catalyst appearing to be concerns around tougher AI regulation, covering both the models themselves and the vast data centre infrastructure required to support them.
“The scale of the falls in some of the market’s biggest names has been striking. But it also highlights the concentration risk that has built up in US equity markets. With a relatively small number of technology and semiconductor stocks now carrying so much weight, weakness in those names quickly translates into sizeable falls for the Nasdaq and S&P 500.
Ahead of this week’s losses, there were plenty of warning signs that markets might have risen too fast.
As my colleague Richard Partington and I wrote in late September, the warning lights were “flashing red” as the fighting in the Middle East intensified, a slowdown loomed in the AI arms race, and government borrowing costs hit multi-decade highs.
One popular measure used by investors to assess whether a market is overvalued – the CAPE ratio – or cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio – had risen to its highest level since 2000 by September, showing that the US stock market is unusually highly valued compared with its profits.
This week’s losses have pulled the CAPE ratio down ( you can see it here ), but it’s still historically high:
Amid the scary-everything-is-bad-in-stocks news, it’s easy to feel a bit worried about pensions or savings, my colleague Siraj Datoo writes.
And yes, yesterday was a bad day in particular for technology stocks, with the Nasdaq losing $2.5tn in market capital in a single day.
But it’s worth taking a second to pause. While many of the charts leading newspaper homepages are fairly narrow, showing the dramatic fall in just a few days, if you look at the Nasdaq, the US index mostly dominated by tech stocks, from the start of the year, it’s still up 4.6% YTD ( see previous post for more details ).
Of course, this correction still could have room to run and markets are famously emotional. But there have been warnings about this. Michael Burry, the famous fund manager behind The Big Short, has been screaming from the sidelines about overvaluations in the tech world.
One of the major concerns right now is the huge data centre buildout in the US and whether Democrats will place restrictions or slow things down. That’s a problem for investors because so many of the world’s biggest companies have invested enormous amounts of money -- often taking on additional debt -- to fund their deep investment. The bet is that the artificial buildout will eventually generate big returns but investors are now increasingly worried about just how long that will take.

articles.title_orig: Paraguay Congress rejects President Pena’s resignation after bank collapse
articles.title_zh: Paraguay Congress rejects President Pena’s resignation after bank collapse
articles.content_orig:
Paraguay’s Congress has refused to accept President Santiago Pena’s resignation, pressing ahead with impeachment proceedings after the collapse of digital lender Ueno Bank.
President since 2023, Pena had attempted to resign on Thursday as millions of Ueno customers remained unable to access their accounts.
“I do so with the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions in mind,” the conservative politician said in a recorded address.
But lawmakers declined to accept his resignation. The lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him, and the Senate opened impeachment proceedings, summoning him to appear on Friday.
A joint congressional session called to consider the resignation lost its quorum after lawmakers from Pena’s Colorado Party walked out, as it became clear there were not enough votes to accept it.
Horacio Cartes, a leader in the Colorado Party, had posted a statement on social media indicating the group supported Pena’s impeachment.
“We will not side with the theft of public, private and pension funds,” Cartes, a former president, wrote in his statement. “We must think of the people and the values we uphold in the Colorado Party.”
Denying Pena’s resignation is likely to heighten the legal jeopardy he faces.
Ordinarily, in Paraguay, presidents who leave office become senators for life, and they enjoy a degree of legal immunity from prosecution as members of the legislature.
But that status is not conferred if the president is convicted in an impeachment trial.
The political crisis erupted earlier this week, when Paraguay’s central bank announced that Ueno had fallen below the legal solvency ratio. Once its books were corrected, the bank’s capital – the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses – was less than half the legal minimum.
Before its collapse, the company claimed it had about 3 million customers, in a country of 6.5 million people. Many have since lost access to their accounts and to pensions paid out through the bank.
As part of a resolution to address the bank’s collapse, Paraguay’s central bank voted to transfer its remaining funds to other financial institutions.
But the central bank itself came under scrutiny for not properly regulating Ueno. The central bank’s head, Carlos Carvallo, has since resigned.
Pena himself formerly held a stake in Ueno’s parent company, Grupo Vazquez, though he said he sold those shares in 2025.
Lawmakers, however, have accused Pena of having a conflict of interest and have questioned whether there was an institutional cover-up linked to the lender’s collapse.
“He is accused of negligence at the very least and complicity in covering up the fact that the bank was insolvent,” said Al Jazeera’s Latin America editor Lucia Newman.
“As I speak, there are people outside urging Congress not to accept the resignation of the president because they say that they want him tried and impeached.”
Until its demise, Ueno had grown quickly from a niche company into a mid-tier bank administering close to $850m in public funds.
Paraguay’s attorney general has also ordered three criminal investigations into the bank’s collapse, which will look into oversight of the lender and the placement of public funds in the institution. Pena has said he will cooperate with investigators.
“My greatest wish is that the return of those funds be guaranteed, that the deposit guarantee fund fulfil its purpose, and that public funds – as well as the resources that belong to all Paraguayans – be protected,” Pena added in his address.
If Pena is ultimately removed from office, Vice President Pedro Alliana would likely take over as president.
Ueno has made no public statement on the issue.

articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment
The Kremlin is weaponizing humanitarian crises Russia itself has created in order to court the Trump Administration. The White House reported on November 5 that First Lady Melania Trump hosted Ukrainian and Russian officials in recognition of the success of the recent limited ceasefire in occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast.[1] Ukraine’s Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and Verkhovna Rada Deputy David Arakhamiya attended the ceremony alongside Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF) CEO Kirill Dmitriev and Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova. Lantratova is notably under US sanctions and has been directly implicated in the kidnapping of at least one Ukrainian child.[2] Dmitriev compared the Oleshky ceasefire to Melania Trump’s previous efforts to repatriate deported Ukrainian children from Russia.[3] Dmitriev highlighted the humanitarian success of the ceasefire without acknowledging that Russia’s invasion and occupation are entirely and solely responsible for the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky.[4] Dmitriev’s comments are in line with previous Russian efforts to use limited humanitarian cooperation — on crises like Oleshky or the return of forcibly deported Ukrainian children, for which Russia itself is uniquely responsible — to court the Trump Administration into adopting a more favorable posture toward Russia and to extract concessions from the United States in future negotiations.[5] Russian officials’ attempts to portray Russian President Vladimir Putin as a willing negotiator with humanitarian inclinations notably follow a string of devastating Russian strikes against Ukrainian civilians in recent months, including a recent strike that killed at least 14 people in Dnipro City while the Oleshky ceasefire was ongoing.[6]
The reported arrest of a prominent Russian milblogger for his coverage of the Oleshky ceasefire is likely part of long-standing Kremlin efforts to censor critical information space actors. Russian media and milbloggers reported on November 5 that Russian authorities arrested prominent Russian military correspondent Vladimir Romanov “Romanov Lite” in connection with his reporting on the humanitarian operation in occupied Oleshky.[7] Romanov reported on October 30, in a now altered post, that 17 buses with evacuated Oleshky residents would travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory and that four would go to Russia, but noted that Russian state media would likely show more buses going to Russia — implying that the Kremlin was planning to deliberately misreport on the humanitarian mission.[8] Romanov has not posted on his Telegram channel since October 31.[9] US outlet Newsmax, the only American outlet allowed into Oleshky, reported that 15 buses left Oleshky, with 11 bound for Ukraine and four to Russia.[10] The Kremlin engaged in a coordinated propaganda campaign intended to present the occupation of Oleshky in a way favorable to Russia in the lead-up to the occupation, and Romanov’s reporting directly undermined those Russian narrative curation efforts.[11] Romanov, one of the last outspoken Russian milbloggers, often criticizes the Russian military command for exaggerating Russian battlefield successes.[12] Russian authorities have long prosecuted and censored Russian milbloggers for speaking against the Kremlin’s false narratives of pervasive Russian battlefield successes, and Romanov’s arrest is likely part of the Kremlin’s efforts to restrict the Russian information space such that only approved pro-Kremlin media figures can retain a platform.[13]
Russia appears to be struggling to export diesel to the United States under the October 9 US-Russia diesel fuel agreement. The Financial Times reported on November 4 that the sanctioned Russian tanker Talisman and the Sierra Leonean-flagged tanker Leruo , initially destined for the US, abruptly changed course on November 2, with the Talisman en route to Brazil while the Leruo steered away from the Atlantic Ocean into the Mediterranean Sea.[14] The Leruo is reportedly signaling “for orders,” indicating that the cargo does not have a confirmed buyer or destination port. Two other tankers carrying Russian diesel are still headed towards the US Atlantic Coast despite signaling that their cargo does not have an official destination port. The four tankers are currently operating without confirmed buyers, as Russia’s ability to successfully offload its diesel at a US port remains unclear. Russia itself is struggling with domestic diesel shortages, which is notable considering there are now four Russian diesel tankers floating in the ocean with no clear destination or buyer.[15] Ukraine’s intensified long-range strike campaign against Russian oil refineries has reduced Russia’s diesel supply domestically and its ability to supply diesel internationally.[16]
The Russian military is continuing the process of forming new maneuver divisions as part of longstanding plans to transition towards a force structure based on divisions and mass. A Russian milblogger published a recruitment advertisement on November 5 claiming that the Russian military command is reorganizing the 6th Motorized Rifle Brigade (3rd Combined Arms Army [CAA], formerly 2nd Luhansk People’s Republic Army Corps [LNR AC], Southern Military District [SMD]) into a division.[17] The reorganization of the 6th Motorized Rifle Brigade follows the recent reformation of the 4th Motorized Rifle Brigade (also of the 3rd CAA) into the 84th Motorized Rifle Division in early October 2026.[18] The 6th Brigade’s reformation, if confirmed, would mean that there are two division-level formations operating under the 3rd CAA, which is generally typical in the structure of a contemporary Russian CAA. The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) has not officially commented on the reorganization as of November 5. The 6th Motorized Rifle Brigade has been operating in the Kramatorsk direction, Donetsk Oblast.[19] The reorganization of the 4th Motorized Rifle Brigade and the 6th Motorized Rifle Brigade into divisions is part of ongoing military reforms that Former Russian Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu announced in December 2022 and brings the total tally of Russian brigades reorganized into maneuver divisions to 13 since 2022.[20] It remains unclear if or how Russia will staff these formations to doctrinal end-strength.
Iran reportedly sought to acquire Russian military equipment in 2023 and 2024 that could support the regime’s counterinsurgency efforts. [NOTE: A version of the following text also appeared in ISW-CTP’s November 5 Iran Update.] Iran purchased at least six Mi-28 helicopters and at least 90 helicopter-mounted, APU-9L guided missile launchers from Russia in 2023 and Spring 2024, respectively, according to documents the Financial Times received from a Ukrainian private intelligence organization.[21] Iranian Deputy Defense and Armed Forces Logistics Minister Mehdi Farahi announced in November 2023 that Iran had “finalized” agreements to purchase at least six Russian Mi-28 helicopters, which can mount APU-9L launchers.[22] An Iranian journalist later shared footage of an Mi-28 in a hangar at an unspecified location in Tehran in January 2026, though it remains unclear whether Iran received the launchers and the guided missiles designated for the launchers.[23] APU-9L launchers are designed for Kh-39 LMUR guided missiles, and it is unclear whether they can accommodate other munitions.[24] The APU-9L system is designed for strikes against stationary and moving targets at ranges of up to 14.5 kilometers, meaning it can be deployed to strike force concentrations, radar stations, or electronic warfare assets, among others.[25] Iran likely sought to acquire these systems to support its counterinsurgency and border security operations, given the system’s limitations.

articles.title_orig: Data centers took a beating in the midterm elections. A reckoning may be ahead for tech giants
articles.title_zh: Data centers took a beating in the midterm elections. A reckoning may be ahead for tech giants
articles.content_orig:
A stunning upset in the Texas governor race and sweeping Democratic victories across the country threaten to curtail the biggest-ever spending boom in US history.
That could disrupt a key growth engine for America’s economy .
Come January, states controlled by Democrats who support expanding or extending AI construction moratoriums will account for 45% of America’s planned data center capacity, according to Goldman Sachs. A quarter of America’s planned AI infrastructure buildout is set to take place in Texas alone.
That doesn’t mean half of America’s planned data centers are on hold. Demand for AI is off the charts. Donald Trump is still president, and he’s already waving around his veto hat. And Democratic governors couldn’t stop every data center from being constructed even if they wanted to.
But Tuesday’s election nevertheless represents a paradigm shift that could alter the pace and path of America’s nonstop AI spending spree – an investment boom that has, according to ING economists, accounted for as much as a quarter of total US economic growth this year.
Communities fighting against the buildings that power AI
Those economic benefits are already real, supporting thousands of jobs. And AI has the potential to revolutionize the way we work.
But an AI data center slowdown could come with important silver linings. It could rein in unfettered growth that has contributed to rebounding inflation and led to widespread public antipathy toward the technology and the data centers that house it. It could also curtail some questionable business models that have raised serious skepticism on Wall Street.
Tapping the brakes could ultimately put AI – and the US economy – on a more sustainable path.
AI infrastructure spending is expected to approach $1 trillion a year, every year, for the foreseeable future, according to Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. As a percentage of America’s gross domestic product, that would outpace every other investment boom in modern US history – including the construction of the railroads.
The outcome of Tuesday’s elections could slow that spending, with vast consequences for the thousands of jobs and massive amounts of economic development that AI supports.
Democrats gained gubernatorial seats in Nevada, Georgia, Ohio and Texas, where candidates campaigned on tightening data center regulations. Proposals from the governors-elect include ending tax breaks, tightening climate and electricity restrictions and allowing local governments to impose their own moratoriums on data center construction.
But Texas is the big kahuna. Wells Fargo estimates that for every 10% reduction in planned Texas data center capacity, Big Tech companies will reduce their AI infrastructure spending by a stunning 1.6% (a lot of money when you’re measuring spending in the trillions of dollars).
State and local politicians have a lot of jurisdiction and sway over that spending: enough to change whether some projects get financed, said Mona Dajani, co-chair of Cooley’s infrastructure, energy and real estate practice.
Hundreds of data center developments that are still awaiting permits, utility service or tax incentives could be particularly exposed, Dajani noted. But even active construction projects could be threatened. Texas law grandfathers in some projects’ permits, protecting them from future changes to local permitting requirements – but that doesn’t resolve state permitting changes or electrical service guarantees that Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa could vacate.
The wait for approvals could add significant costs for AI companies, Dajani said: Interest, equipment commitments and utility expenses will all continue to accrue, even while a project is on ice. At some point, existing projects could stop being financially viable.
If that happens, AI companies – who have already strained to build out data centers fast enough to meet their anticipated demand – may not be able to meet their explosive spending targets.
“This is a rare case where state and local leaders have influence of geopolitical-level import,” said Harry Krejsa, director of studies at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology.
Data centers aren’t exclusively a Democratic issue: Americans have displayed bipartisan consensus for putting guardrails around data center buildouts.
Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott had already imposed a data center moratorium that Hinojosa campaigned on extending until lawmakers establish stronger AI regulations.
But Trump had railed against any attempts to stymie AI’s growth and spending, citing economic and national security – particularly in the high-stakes race against China. Many Republican politicians who may have otherwise supported AI regulations, including frameworks for data center construction, remained silent.
Still, there’s evidence that the AI buildout could be on an unsustainable path.
The United States had 5,427 data centers at the end of last year, according to Stanford University’s AI Index Report , and AI companies have announced plans for 3,969 new US data centers, according to Aterio , a data center research company. But only about 800 are under construction, and AI experts have raised doubts about the viability of many of the announced projects.
If Tuesday’s election results trigger an investment slowdown, that could trim some of the industry’s fat.
Example A: CoreWeave, a neocloud business that rents out computing capacity, recently projected such extensive losses that its bond yields surged to 15% – the danger zone. That was particularly troubling, because its expected return on investment was only around 9%.
In other words, CoreWeave loses money on every single dollar it spends on expanding its data center capacity.
Deep-pocketed hyperscalers – Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft – don’t have that problem. But their stocks have been slammed in recent weeks as investors grow impatient with what they view as an unsustainable amount of spending that may not return profits for years.
“AI is catching a break here,” said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM US.
Brusuelas expects growth to slow from last quarter’s 3.4% pace to something closer to 2.4% if there is an AI slowdown. That’s still solid long-term growth. And America’s economy is massive and diverse. Investment that otherwise would have gone to data centers can go elsewhere.
“It’s slowing, but it doesn’t mean we’re going to have a recession,” Brusuelas said.
It also presents an opportunity for AI companies to get smart about their future AI data center rollouts – and get put on a more sustainable course.
The helter-skelter approach to data center construction has resulted in significant amounts of money getting flushed down the toilet in unworkable projects – collateral damage from massive competition to be first and biggest. Data centers already face $200 billion in project delays, according to Mike Mathews, global digital infrastructure practice leader at risk adviser Marsh.
A more rational, politically sensitive approach could create longer-term benefits for the communities that host the data centers and for the AI companies themselves.
There’s precedent for that. In the previous decade, the Googles of the world built out data centers for the cloud computing revolution, promoting the fact that they’d be built sustainably with renewable energy – even before it was cost-effective to do that. A similar, community-based approach could provide AI companies with the compute they need and give them the political and social license to operate their data centers for the long haul.
“Like the saying goes: If you want to go fast, you go it alone; if you want to go far you go together,” said Krejsa. “If you squander political license to operate at home, that’ll be a bigger impediment to remaining competitive with China.”
